text: You can already add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers algebraically — but a plus b i form hides something important: complex numbers have a natural picture, and that picture is exactly how physicists talk about a qubit's phase.

Plot a plus b i as a point on the complex plane: the horizontal axis is the real part, the vertical axis is the imaginary part. Instead of describing that point by how far right and how far up, you can describe it by its modulus, r, the straight-line distance from the origin, and its argument, theta, the angle from the positive real axis. These formulas convert rectangular form into this polar form.

Take z equals 3 plus 4i again. Its modulus is the square root of 9 plus 16, which is the square root of 25, exactly 5. Its argument comes out to roughly 53.13 degrees. Checking it: 5 times cosine of 53.13 degrees is about 3, and 5 times sine of 53.13 degrees is about 4 — recovering the original number exactly.

Euler's formula states that e to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta — a complex number of modulus exactly 1, sitting at angle theta. Going the other direction, from polar to rectangular: with r equals 2 and theta equals 60 degrees, the real part is 2 times cosine 60, which is 1, and the imaginary part is 2 times sine 60, about 1.732.

A general qubit state is alpha ket-zero plus beta ket-one, and because each amplitude is complex, each one has its own argument — exactly what physicists call phase. A global phase, rotating both amplitudes by the same angle, turns out to be unobservable. A relative phase — a difference in angle between the two amplitudes — is physically real, and it's a big part of why quantum computing can do things classical bits cannot.

Next lesson uses a second route to the modulus — multiplying a complex number by its own mirror image — which turns out to be the exact calculation quantum computing uses to turn an amplitude into a probability.
